title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
Urban mobility refers to the movement of people and goods within and between cities, spanning all modes of transport such as walking, cycling, public transit, private vehicles, and freight. Driven by factors like population growth and climate change, urban mobility planning aims to create smart, efficient, and sustainable networks that reduce congestion and emissions while enhancing quality of life and economic vitality. Key developments include the rise of shared mobility services, autonomous vehicles, and integrated smart systems that prioritize user experience, safety, and inclusivity in urban environments.
As city-wide urban infrastructures such as buses, taxis, mass rapid transit, public utilities and roads become digital, the datasets obtained can be used as a framework for tracking movement patterns through space and time. This is especially true with the widespread deployment of pervasive computing technologies such as smart cards, GPS, and RFID in vehicles. For example, routes and ridership data were collected with the use of smart cards and Global Positioning System (GPS) devices available on the public buses. These large-scale movement datasets often contain patterns that reveal important characteristics of urban mobility. Identifying and analyzing such patterns can deepen our understanding of human mobility, supporting better urban management. For both public and private transport providers, these insights enable more informed decisions and improved service planning.
In real-world practices, the use of these massive locational aware data to gain better urban mobility patterns and trends, however, tend to be confined to simple tracking and mapping with GIS applications. This is mainly because conventional GIS tools lack robust geospatial statistics capabilities for analyzing and modeling spatial and spatio-temporal data.

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
Aspatial data
For the purpose of this take-home exercise, the latest month Passenger Volume by Origin Destination Bus Stops downloaded from LTA DataMall will be used.

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
Geospatial data
Two geospatial data will be used in this study, they are:

Bus Stop Location from LTA DataMall. It provides information about all the bus stops currently being serviced by buses, including the bus stop code (identifier) and location coordinates.
Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) from Singapore’s open data portal.

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
Importing the Study Area
We import the Master Plan 2019 Subzone polygons, drop any Z/M dimensions that aren’t needed for 2D analysis and transform the data into SVY21/EPSG:3414 which is the common projected CRS used for Singapore. Using a consistent projected CRS ensures distance or area calculations and overlays behave correctly.
Using SVY21 / EPSG:3414 standardises all geometry into a projected CRS suitable for distance and area operations in Singapore. Dropping Z/M ensures a clean 2D topology so overlays, contiguity, and grid generation behave as expected.
The following code chunk will import the masterplan data, removes the Z (elevation) and M (measure) dimension, and transforms into SVY21.

#|eval: false
mpsz_sf <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml") %>% 
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>% st_transform(crs = 3414)

  using driver `KML'

Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6057 ymin: 1.158699 xmax: 104.0885 ymax: 1.470775
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84


Outlying islands are excluded to keep the analysis focused on the contiguous urban network of the main island where bus services and OD demand are dense and comparable.
The following code chunk will be use to filter the unwanted areas as we will be focused on the main island of Singapore.

#|eval: false
extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

mpsz_sf <- mpsz_sf %>%
  mutate(
    REGION_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),
    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
  ) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())

mpsz_cl <- mpsz_sf %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N != "SOUTHERN GROUP",
         PLN_AREA_N != "WESTERN ISLANDS",
         PLN_AREA_N != "NORTH-EASTERN ISLANDS")


#|eval: false
#|echo: false
write_rds(mpsz_cl, 
          "data/rds/mpsz_cl.rds")


#|echo: false
mpsz_cl <- read_rds("data/rds/mpsz_cl.rds")

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
section: Extracting the Bus Stops within Singapore
text:
Extracting the Bus Stops within Singapore
Not all bus stops in the LTA dataset are located within the main island. In this step, we perform a spatial join between the bus stop data and the Master Plan subzones to keep only those bus stops located within the mainland boundary. This ensures that our later analysis only includes relevant bus stops in Singapore’s main island.

BusStop_in_SG <- st_join(
  BusStop, mpsz_cl,
  join = st_within,
  left = FALSE)


#|eval: false
#|echo: false
write_rds(BusStop_in_SG, 
          "data/rds/busstop.rds")


#|echo: false
BusStop_in_SG <- read_rds("data/rds/busstop.rds")







Important



Keeping only stops that fall within the main island prevents stray records (depots or offshore stops) from entering the analysis. This also makes neighbour structures more regular along the coastline.

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
Cleaning the Grid
Clipping can introduce tiny geometry issues or empty pieces. Here we make geometries valid and drop any empty cells. This keeps later neighbour building stable.

hex_grid <- hex_grid %>%
  st_make_valid() %>%
  filter(!st_is_empty(st_geometry(.)))

nrow(hex_grid)

[1] 3254

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
Giving Each Hexagon an ID
Local statistics and joins are much easier when every zone has a stable key. We add a running ID to the grid that we will carry through the whole workflow.

hex_grid <- hex_grid %>%
  mutate(hex_id = row_number()) %>%
  relocate(hex_id)

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
section: Creating a Canonical Hexagon Base and Spatial Weights
text:
Creating a Canonical Hexagon Base and Spatial Weights
We define how each hexagon relates to nearby cells using queen contiguity (touching by edge or corner) and convert those relationships into row-standardised weights. This provides the local context Gi* and Moran’s I need to judge whether a hexagon sits inside a cluster of similarly high or low values.
We use queen contiguity to capture both edge- and corner-touching neighbours, which is standard for hex grids and avoids over-sparse networks. For Gi* we include self-neighbours, while for Local Moran’s I we intentionally exclude self so the cell is compared to its surroundings. Weights are row-standardised (W) so each cell contributes equally regardless of its degree.

hex_base <- hex_grid

nb_q <- st_contiguity(hex_base)

has_nb <- card(nb_q) > 0
hex_base <- hex_base[has_nb, ]

nb_q <- st_contiguity(hex_base)

lw_q <- st_weights(nb_q, style = "W")

nb_star <- include_self(nb_q)
lw_star <- nb2listw(nb_star, style = "W")
wt_star <- lw_star$weights
# ---------------------------------------------

summary(card(nb_q))

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  1.000   6.000   6.000   6.634   8.000  15.000

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
Visualising Neighbour Counts
A simple neighbour count map helps confirm that contiguity looks reasonable and highlights edge cells with fewer links.

hex_base <- hex_base %>% mutate(n_nb = card(nb_q))

tmap_mode("plot")

tm_shape(hex_base) +
  tm_polygons(col = "n_nb", 
              palette = "Blues", 
              title = "Neighbour count") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.4) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








Interior cells cluster around 6–8 neighbours. Lower counts along coasts signal edge effects; row-standardising helps reduce their influence in the local statistics.

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
Linking origin stops to hexagons
We join each origin stop code to the hexagon that contains it, using the lookup already created. We keep only origin codes that successfully match a hex ID so that we can aggregate trips by hexagon and period.

ori_lookup <- stops_hex %>% rename(ORI = BUS_STOP_N, hex_id_o = hex_id)

od_ohex <- od %>%
  left_join(ori_lookup, by = "ORI") %>%
  filter(!is.na(hex_id_o))

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
Defining the three time windows
We tag each record into one of the three study windows. Weekday morning is hours 6 to 8, weekday afternoon is hours 17 to 19 and weekend or holiday is hours 11 to 19. This will help reflect distinct travel behaviours, morning commute origins, evening return flows and diffuse leisure activity.
The following code chunk will label each OD record into one of the three study windows.

od_tagged <- od_ohex %>%
  mutate(
    DTYPE_C = toupper(trimws(DTYPE)),
    DTYPE_C = case_when(
    DTYPE_C == "WEEKDAY" ~ "WEEKDAY",
    grepl("WEEKEND", DTYPE_C) | grepl("HOLIDAY", DTYPE_C) ~ "WEEKEND",
    TRUE ~ DTYPE_C
    ),
    PERIOD = case_when(
    DTYPE_C == "WEEKDAY"  & HOUR %in% 6:8   ~ "AM peak",
    DTYPE_C == "WEEKDAY"  & HOUR %in% 17:19 ~ "PM peak",
    DTYPE_C == "WEEKEND"  & HOUR %in% 11:19 ~ "Weekend",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )
) %>%
filter(!is.na(PERIOD))

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
section: Summarising origin-generated trips at hexagon level
text:
Summarising origin-generated trips at hexagon level
We sum trips by origin hexagon within each period and join the totals back to the canonical grid. Missing combinations are set to zero so every zone has a valid value and maps and statistics are computed on the same geometry.

hex_trips <- od_tagged %>%
  group_by(hex_id_o, PERIOD) %>%
summarise(TRIPS = sum(TRIPS, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
rename(hex_id = hex_id_o)

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
section: Joining totals back to the canonical grid
text:
Joining totals back to the canonical grid
We create three hex layers, one for each period, based on the same canonical grid used to build neighbours and weights. Missing values are set to zero so every zone has a numeric value.

hex_am <- hex_base %>%
  left_join(filter(hex_trips, PERIOD == "AM peak") %>% select(hex_id, TRIPS),
  by = "hex_id") %>%
  mutate(TRIPS = ifelse(is.na(TRIPS), 0, as.numeric(TRIPS)))

hex_pm <- hex_base %>%
  left_join(filter(hex_trips, PERIOD == "PM peak") %>% select(hex_id, TRIPS),
  by = "hex_id") %>%
  mutate(TRIPS = ifelse(is.na(TRIPS), 0, as.numeric(TRIPS)))

hex_wknd <- hex_base %>%
  left_join(filter(hex_trips, PERIOD == "Weekend") %>% select(hex_id, TRIPS),
  by = "hex_id") %>%
  mutate(TRIPS = ifelse(is.na(TRIPS), 0, as.numeric(TRIPS)))

Using summary() we can check if the layers created are in order.

summary(hex_am$TRIPS)

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
LMSA - Getis-Ord Gi*
We use Local Getis–Ord Gi* to detect clusters of high (hot) and low (cold) origin trip intensity, accounting for each hexagon’s neighbours (queen contiguity, row-standardized, self-included). The continuous z-score map shows gradients; the banded map flags only statistically reliable clusters (90/95/99%). Gi* is our primary measure because it answers the planning question “Where are sustained concentrations of origin demand?“

lw_q_listw <- nb2listw(nb_q, style = "W")
wt_q <- lw_q_listw$weights
set.seed(2025)

The following code chunk will be used to define our classifier helper to be used for each period. Gi* measures whether a hexagon sits inside a local concentration of high values (hot spot) or low values (cold spot), given its neighbours. We compute Gi* and translate the z-scores into simple significance bands (90/95/99%) so the maps clearly mark statistically meaningful clusters.

gi_compute_classify <- function(hex_sf, value_col = "TRIPS", nsim = 499) {
  gi <- local_gstar_perm(
    x  = as.numeric(hex_sf[[value_col]]),
    nb = nb_star,
    wt = wt_star,
    nsim = nsim
  )
  out <- bind_cols(hex_sf, gi)

  out |>
    mutate(
      gi_band = case_when(
        gi_star >= 2.58  ~ "Hot spot (99%)",
        gi_star >= 1.96  ~ "Hot spot (95%)",
        gi_star >= 1.65  ~ "Hot spot (90%)",
        gi_star <= -2.58 ~ "Cold spot (99%)",
        gi_star <= -1.96 ~ "Cold spot (95%)",
        gi_star <= -1.65 ~ "Cold spot (90%)",
        TRUE             ~ "Not significant"
      ),
      gi_band = factor(gi_band, levels = c(
        "Hot spot (99%)","Hot spot (95%)","Hot spot (90%)",
        "Not significant",
        "Cold spot (90%)","Cold spot (95%)","Cold spot (99%)"
      ))
    )
}


gi_am   <- gi_compute_classify(hex_am)
gi_pm   <- gi_compute_classify(hex_pm)
gi_wknd <- gi_compute_classify(hex_wknd)


Weekday AM PeakWeekday PM PeakWeekend/Holiday



tmap_mode("plot")
tm_shape(gi_am) +
  tm_polygons(col = "gi_star", 
              palette = "RdBu", 
              style = "pretty",
              title = "AM peak: Local Gi* (z)") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.4) + tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








During the morning peak, most hexagons display neutral Gi* z-scores close to zero, suggesting that trip generation intensity is generally consistent across the island. However, several clusters of higher z-scores are observed in the north-eastern and eastern parts of Singapore, indicating local concentrations of heavy boarding activity in large residential towns. A smaller patch of elevated z-values appears in the western region. These blue-toned areas represent potential hot spot zones where multiple neighbouring hexagons share high trip counts. In contrast, negative or cold z-values are minimal and scattered, implying that there are few areas with significantly lower trip activity relative to their surroundings.

tm_shape(gi_am) +
  tm_polygons(col = "gi_band",
              palette = c("#990000","#d7301f","#fc8d59","#d9d9d9","#91bfdb","#4575b4","#313695"),
              title = "AM peak: Hot/Cold significance") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.4) + tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








During the weekday morning peak, several statistically significant hot spots emerge across the eastern, north-eastern and western regions of Singapore. These clusters coincide with residential areas where many passengers begin their morning commutes. The concentration of high trip volumes within adjacent hexagons confirms strong local clustering of boarding activity. In contrast, no cold spots are detected. This is expected as central business districts are surrounded by moderate-activity areas that prevent them from forming statistically significant low-value clusters. Overall, the morning map shows distinct and consistent zones of high origin intensity, reflecting concentrated commuter flows from residential areas toward the city.



tmap_mode("plot")
tm_shape(gi_pm) +
  tm_polygons(col = "gi_star", 
              palette = "RdBu", 
              style = "pretty",
              title = "PM peak: Local Gi* (z)") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.4) + tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








In the evening peak, the spatial pattern of Gi* z-scores remains similar to the morning but with generally weaker intensities. Blue-shaded areas persist in the eastern and north-eastern zones, though they appear more fragmented and less pronounced. This reflects the dispersion of return trips from employment centres toward residential areas, resulting in a more balanced distribution of trip origins. Most hexagons remain in neutral shades, showing that overall spatial clustering of trip generation is modest during the afternoon period.

tm_shape(gi_pm) +
  tm_polygons(col = "gi_band",
              palette = c("#990000","#d7301f","#fc8d59","#d9d9d9","#91bfdb","#4575b4","#313695"),
              title = "PM peak: Hot/Cold significance") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.4) + tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








In the evening peak, hot spots remain visible across similar residential regions in the east and west but appear more spatially dispersed compared to the morning pattern. This dispersion reflects the return flow of commuters departing from various work locations and spreading across multiple residential destinations. The reduced clustering strength indicates that trip origins are more balanced across the network during the PM period. As in the morning, no cold spots are identified which suggests that low-origin areas are interspersed among moderate zones rather than forming distinct low-value clusters. The spatial pattern is therefore less polarized but still highlights key commuter corridors linked to the housing estates.



tmap_mode("plot")
tm_shape(gi_wknd) +
  tm_polygons(col = "gi_star", 
              palette = "RdBu", 
              style = "pretty",
              title = "Weekend/Holiday: Local Gi* (z)") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.4) + tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








The weekend and holiday pattern exhibits the weakest clustering among all periods. Most hexagons fall within neutral z-score ranges, suggesting that trip generation is relatively even across the island. Only a few small blue patches are visible, mainly around suburban centres in the east and north-east. These areas likely represent localised concentrations linked to leisure or shopping activities. The overall spatial pattern appears diffuse, indicating that weekend travel is less structured and more evenly distributed compared to weekday commuting flows.

tm_shape(gi_wknd) +
  tm_polygons(col = "gi_band",
              palette = c("#990000","#d7301f","#fc8d59","#d9d9d9","#91bfdb","#4575b4","#313695"),
              title = "Weekend/Holiday: Hot/Cold significance") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.4) + tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








Weekend and holiday travel displays a similar but more diffuse pattern of hot spots with clusters again appearing in the eastern, north-eastern and western parts of Singapore. These areas correspond to major suburban centres and recreational hubs where leisure and shopping activities would attract higher trip volumes. The overall clustering strength is weaker than on weekdays, consistent with more irregular and dispersed travel behaviour. As with the weekday periods, no cold spots are observed, reaffirming that trip generation remains relatively even across the island with few areas consistently exhibiting low values. This reflects the more balanced, non-directional nature of weekend mobility.



Across all three periods, the Getis–Ord Gi* results reveal a consistent spatial structure of hot spot clusters in major residential regions located in the east, north-east and west parts of Singapore. These areas represent key trip-origin zones where large populations generate high volumes of bus boardings.
The clustering is strongest during the weekday morning peak, when commuting flows are highly directional from residential estates toward central employment zones. In the evening peak, hot spots remain in similar regions but become more scattered, reflecting commuters returning home through multiple routes. During weekends and holidays, hot spot intensity weakens further and spreads more evenly across the island, consistent with dispersed leisure and social travel.
The absence of significant cold spots throughout all periods indicates that trip generation is generally well distributed, with few areas persistently exhibiting low activity. Overall, the spatial pattern highlights Singapore’s clear residential-to-central commuting structure and the stability of high-demand zones across different time frames.






Important



The absence of cold spots is not a data or coding error. It arises naturally from the context and data type:

The analysis focuses on origin trips, which are inherently higher in residential zones and more evenly distributed elsewhere.
The central and commercial regions, though low in origins, are surrounded by mixed-use or moderate zones, preventing them from forming statistically distinct “cold clusters.”
Row-standardised weights and self-included neighbours also dampen low-value z-scores, meaning weak negatives rarely cross significance thresholds.

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
LMSA - Local Moran’s
Local Moran’s I is used as a supporting diagnostic to complement the Getis–Ord Gi* analysis. While Gi* identifies local concentrations of high or low trip intensity (hot and cold clusters), Local Moran’s I focuses on measuring spatial association (how similar or dissimilar a hexagon’s trip count is compared to its neighbours). It helps reveal spatial outliers such as unusually high cells surrounded by low values (High–Low) or low cells among high values (Low–High).

Weekday AM PeakWeekday PM PeakWeekend/Holiday



Local Moran’s I

Local Moran’s I Cluster Map


Having identified the degree of spatial association in the previous step, we now categorize the Local Moran’s I results into meaningful cluster types. This helps to visualize where significant spatial groupings or outliers occur across Singapore.

hex_am_lisa_sig <- hex_am_lisa %>%
mutate(
  cluster_type = case_when(
  p_ii < 0.05 & lag_z > 0 & z > 0 ~ "High-High",
  p_ii < 0.05 & lag_z < 0 & z < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
  p_ii < 0.05 & lag_z > 0 & z < 0 ~ "Low-High",
  p_ii < 0.05 & lag_z < 0 & z > 0 ~ "High-Low",
  TRUE ~ "Not Significant"
  )
)


tm_shape(hex_am_lisa_sig) +
  tm_polygons(
  col = "cluster_type",
  palette = c("red", "blue", "orange", "lightblue", "grey"),
  title = "LISA Cluster Map – AM Peak Trips"
  ) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








The AM peak map shows several distinct High–High (HH) clusters concentrated in the east, north-east and west of Singapore. These correspond to areas where high trip counts are surrounded by similarly high neighbours which are primarily large residential estates generating strong morning boarding activity. A few Low–High (LH) outliers appear nearby, representing zones with lower trip counts adjacent to high-activity areas, likely small stops within otherwise busy residential corridors. These patterns align closely with the earlier Local Moran’s I values, which indicated moderate positive spatial autocorrelation in the same regions. The overall result confirms that morning trips form stable and concentrated clusters of high activity, consistent with directional commuter flows from residential to central areas.






The afternoon period reflects the return flow from employment areas to residential areas. We repeat the same steps used for the morning peak so that results are comparable. First we make sure the trip column has no missing values. Then we compute Local Moran’s I using the same queen contiguity neighbours and the same row-standardised weights. Finally we map the statistic and produce a LISA cluster map that classifies each hexagon into high–high, low–low, or outlier types based on significance.

Local Moran’s I

hex_pm <- hex_pm %>%
  mutate(TRIPS = as.numeric(TRIPS),
         TRIPS = ifelse(is.na(TRIPS), 0, TRIPS))

pm_lisa <- local_moran(
  x  = hex_pm$TRIPS,
  nb = nb_q,
  wt = wt_q,
  nsim = 499
)

pm_lisa <- pm_lisa %>%
  mutate(
    z     = scale(hex_pm$TRIPS)[, 1],
    lag_z = lag.listw(lw_q_listw, z)
)

hex_pm_lisa <- bind_cols(hex_pm, pm_lisa)


tm_shape(hex_pm_lisa) +
  tm_polygons(col = "ii",
              palette = "RdBu",
              title = "Local Moran’s I") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.4) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








In the evening period, the spatial autocorrelation remains generally weak, similar to the AM pattern. Most cells have near-zero values, indicating little to no local dependency in trip generation. However, small pockets of higher positive values appear around the eastern and western residential regions, reflecting continued spatial similarity among neighbouring high-trip zones. Negative values are sparse and scattered, showing limited contrast between adjacent cells. This suggests that while commuting flows return toward residential areas, the degree of local clustering is less intense than during the morning peak.


Local Moran’s I Cluster Map

pm_lisa_sig <- hex_pm_lisa %>%
  mutate(
    cluster_type = case_when(
      p_ii < 0.05 & lag_z > 0 & z > 0 ~ "High-High",
      p_ii < 0.05 & lag_z < 0 & z < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
      p_ii < 0.05 & lag_z > 0 & z < 0 ~ "Low-High",
      p_ii < 0.05 & lag_z < 0 & z > 0 ~ "High-Low",
      TRUE ~ "Not Significant"),
    cluster_type = factor(
    cluster_type,
    levels = c("High-High","Low-Low","Low-High","High-Low","Not Significant")
  )
)


tm_shape(pm_lisa_sig) +
  tm_polygons(
  col = "cluster_type",
  palette = c("High-High" = "red",
  "Low-Low"   = "blue",
  "Low-High"  = "royalblue3",
  "High-Low"  = "orange",
  "Not Significant" = "goldenrod"),
  title = "LISA Cluster Map – PM Peak Trips"
) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.4) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








During the PM peak, High–High clusters persist in the same residential regions identified during the morning, though they appear smaller and more scattered. This suggests that while evening return trips remain concentrated around major housing estates, the spatial pattern is more dispersed due to multiple route options and staggered travel times. A few Low–Low (LL) and Low–High (LH) relationships emerge, indicating areas of weaker spatial association or minor contrasts between adjacent cells. Compared to the earlier Moran’s I plot, these clusters correspond with zones that maintained moderate positive values but at lower magnitudes, reflecting a gentler evening spatial pattern.



The weekend and holiday period captures non-commuting travel behaviour that differs substantially from weekday movement. Unlike the structured flows seen during morning and afternoon peaks, weekend trips are driven mainly by leisure, retail, and social activities. We apply the same analytical procedure used for weekday periods to ensure consistency. After confirming that all trip values are numeric and complete, Local Moran’s I is computed using the same queen contiguity neighbours and row-standardised spatial weights.

Local Moran’s I

wknd_lisa <- local_moran(
  x  = hex_wknd$TRIPS,
  nb = nb_q,
  wt = wt_q,
  nsim = 499
  )

wknd_lisa <- wknd_lisa %>%
  mutate(
    z = scale(hex_wknd$TRIPS)[, 1],
    lag_z = lag.listw(lw_q_listw, z)
)

hex_wknd_lisa <- bind_cols(hex_wknd, wknd_lisa)


tm_shape(hex_wknd_lisa) +
  tm_polygons(col = "ii", 
              palette = "RdBu", 
              title = "Local Moran’s I") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.4) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








The weekend and holiday map displays the weakest overall autocorrelation among all periods. The vast majority of hexagons fall within near-zero ranges, implying that trip intensity varies independently between locations. Only small clusters in the east and west exhibit modest positive values, pointing to localised zones of similar boarding levels, likely related to leisure and shopping activity. Negative values remain minimal and isolated, suggesting little spatial contrast. The pattern reinforces the view that weekend travel is more diffuse and less spatially structured than weekday commuting flows.


Local Moran’s I Cluster Map

wknd_lisa_sig <- hex_wknd_lisa %>%
  mutate(
    cluster_type = case_when(
      p_ii < 0.05 & lag_z > 0 & z > 0 ~ "High-High",
      p_ii < 0.05 & lag_z < 0 & z < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
      p_ii < 0.05 & lag_z > 0 & z < 0 ~ "Low-High",
      p_ii < 0.05 & lag_z < 0 & z > 0 ~ "High-Low",
      TRUE ~ "Not Significant"),
    cluster_type = factor(
    cluster_type,
    levels = c("High-High","Low-Low","Low-High","High-Low","Not Significant")
  )
)


tm_shape(wknd_lisa_sig) +
  tm_polygons(
    col = "cluster_type",
    palette = c(
    "High-High" = "red",
    "Low-Low" = "blue",
    "Low-High" = "royalblue3",
    "High-Low" = "orange",
    "Not Significant"= "goldenrod"),
    title = "LISA Cluster Map – Weekend/Holiday Trips") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.4) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








On weekends and holidays, the High–High clusters remain in similar areas as the weekday periods but appear more widely spread and less intense. These likely correspond to suburban centres and leisure destinations attracting consistent passenger activity. Scattered Low–High pockets are visible around these clusters, suggesting a mix of high- and low-demand stops within close proximity, typical of diverse weekend travel purposes. The map aligns with the earlier Local Moran’s I results, which showed generally weak spatial autocorrelation and limited clustering strength. Overall, the weekend pattern illustrates more balanced and flexible travel behaviour with localised concentrations but fewer strong clusters compared to weekday commuting.










Note



The Local Moran’s I and LISA cluster maps reveal that weekday AM trips exhibit the strongest and most cohesive spatial clustering, while PM and weekend trips become progressively weaker and more dispersed. The correlation between the high positive Moran’s I values and the High–High LISA clusters confirms that residential areas are consistently the key drivers of trip generation across all time periods.


The Local Moran’s I results complement the Gi* findings by revealing how spatial clusters and outliers relate within the same underlying travel pattern. While the Gi* analysis focuses on identifying areas of consistently high or low trip intensity (hot and cold spots), Local Moran’s I highlights the relationships among neighbouring cells by distinguishing between strongly correlated clusters (High–High, Low–Low) and contrasting outliers (High–Low, Low–High).
Together, both methods confirm that weekday morning trips form clear and cohesive clusters in major residential zones, while evening and weekend trips are more spatially dispersed. The agreement between the two measures strengthens the conclusion that Singapore’s trip-generation pattern is spatially structured yet time-dependent, with the intensity and clustering of demand varying across different travel periods.
Taken together, the LMSA maps identify where trip generation clusters consistently. EHSA then tests whether those clusters are strengthening or weakening over time.

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
section: Mann-Kendall Test using the spatio-temporal local Gi* values
text:
Mann-Kendall Test using the spatio-temporal local Gi* values

Combining the datasets
We downloaded the data of Passenger Volume by Origin Destination Bus Stops for the past 3 months (Jul, Aug, Sept) and will proceed to combine the datasets into one.

od_202507 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/origin_destination_bus_202507.csv")
od_202508 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/origin_destination_bus_202508.csv")
od_202509 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/origin_destination_bus_202509.csv")

od_all <- bind_rows(od_202507, od_202508, od_202509)


#|echo: false
od_all <- read_rds("data/rds/od_all.rds")



Extract and aggregate by month
We will use the YEAR_MONTH field to separate the data using the following code chunk.

od_all <- od_all %>%
  mutate(YEAR_MONTH = as.character(YEAR_MONTH)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(ORIGIN_PT_CODE), !is.na(TOTAL_TRIPS))



Aggregate by origin and month

od_monthly <- od_all %>%
  mutate(YEAR_MONTH = as.character(YEAR_MONTH)) %>%
  group_by(ORIGIN_PT_CODE, YEAR_MONTH) %>%
  summarise(TRIPS = sum(TOTAL_TRIPS, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")



Attach to hex grid

od_hex <- od_monthly %>%
  left_join(stops_hex %>% rename(ORI = BUS_STOP_N, hex_id = hex_id),
            by = c("ORIGIN_PT_CODE" = "ORI")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(hex_id))



Build complete hex-month panel
We first aggregate total trips for each month by origin hexagon. Some hexagons may not register trips every month, so we fill missing combinations with 0. This ensures every cell has a valid value before computing Local Gi*.

all_hex <- hex_base$hex_id

months_avail <- sort(unique(od_all$YEAR_MONTH))
months_avail <- factor(months_avail, levels = months_avail)

hex_time <- od_hex %>%
  group_by(hex_id, YEAR_MONTH) %>%
  summarise(TRIPS = sum(TRIPS, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  complete(hex_id = all_hex, YEAR_MONTH = months_avail, fill = list(TRIPS = 0))



Join back to hex geometry
We link the completed table back to the canonical hexagon grid so that each record again carries its polygon geometry. By copying the geometry from the grid using the hex_id, we preserve the simple-features structure and ensure the data is ready for spatial analysis and mapping.

hex_time <- hex_time %>%
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(hex_base), by = "hex_id")

st_geometry(hex_time) <- st_geometry(hex_base)[match(hex_time$hex_id, hex_base$hex_id)]
st_crs(hex_time) <- st_crs(hex_base)



Compute monthly Local Gi*
For each month separately, we compute the Local Getis-Ord Gi* statistic using the same queen contiguity neighbours and row-standardised weights as before. Before computing, we reorder the month’s rows to match the grid’s neighbour indexing so the data vector aligns exactly with the spatial weights. Gi* highlights where each hexagon forms a local concentration of high (hot) or low (cold) values relative to its neighbours.

gi_list <- months_avail %>%
  map(~{
    m <- .
    data <- hex_time %>%
      filter(YEAR_MONTH == m) %>%
      mutate(hex_id = factor(hex_id, levels = all_hex)) %>%
      arrange(hex_id)

    gi <- local_gstar_perm(
      x  = data$TRIPS,
      nb = nb_star,
      wt = wt_star,
      nsim = 499
    )

    bind_cols(data, gi %>% select(gi_star))
  })

hex_gi_time <- bind_rows(gi_list) %>%
  mutate(YEAR_MONTH = factor(YEAR_MONTH, levels = months_avail))



Mann–Kendall Trend Test
We now test whether each hexagon’s Local Gi* values are increasing or decreasing across the three months. The Mann-Kendall test is a non-parametric test for monotonic trends. A positive Kendall’s τ (tau) indicates an increasing trend (emerging hot spot), while a negative τ indicates a decreasing trend (diminishing hot spot).
Hypotheses:

H₀ (Null Hypothesis): There is no monotonic trend in the Local Gi* values.
H₁ (Alternative Hypothesis): A monotonic trend exists, either increasing or decreasing.

Interpretation:

Reject the null hypothesis if the p-value is smaller than the significance level (commonly 0.05).
The Kendall’s tau (τ) value ranges from –1 to +1:

τ = +1 - perfectly increasing trend (consistent upward change)
τ = –1 - perfectly decreasing trend (consistent downward change)
τ ≈ 0 - no clear trend or random fluctuations



mk_summarise <- function(x) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  
  if (length(x) < 3 || length(unique(x)) < 2) {
    return(tibble(tau = NA_real_, p_value = NA_real_))
  }
  
  out <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(seq_along(x), x, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE))
  tibble(
    tau     = unname(out$estimate),
    p_value = out$p.value
  )
}

gi_trend <- hex_gi_time %>%
  arrange(hex_id, YEAR_MONTH) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(hex_id) %>%
  summarise(
    gi_vec = list(gi_star[order(YEAR_MONTH)]),
    gi_latest = last(gi_star[order(YEAR_MONTH)]),
    gi_mean = mean(gi_star, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(mk = map(gi_vec, mk_summarise)) %>%
  unnest_wider(mk)

To verify that the Mann–Kendall trend analysis has run successfully, we use head() to preview the first few rows of the results table. This simple check helps confirm that the new columns tau and p_value were created correctly for each hexagon.

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
section: Classifying Emerging and Diminishing Hot Spots
text:
Classifying Emerging and Diminishing Hot Spots
After performing the Mann–Kendall test, we map the results to visualize spatial trends in Local Gi* values across Singapore. Each hexagon is classified as an emerging, diminishing or non-significant hot spot based on the tau and p-value results.

gi_trend <- gi_trend %>%
  mutate(
    trend_type = case_when(
      p_value < 0.05 & tau > 0  ~ "Emerging Hot Spot",
      p_value < 0.05 & tau < 0  ~ "Diminishing Hot Spot",
      p_value >= 0.05           ~ "No Significant Trend"
    )
  )


Join Geometry for Mapping
Before visualization, we reattach the canonical hexagon geometries to the classified trend data. This ensures that each record can be spatially represented on the map.

gi_trend <- gi_trend %>%
  mutate(hex_id = as.integer(as.character(hex_id)))

hex_ehsa <- hex_base %>%
  left_join(
    gi_trend %>%
      select(hex_id, 
             trend_type, 
             tau, p_value, 
             gi_latest, 
             gi_mean
             ),
    by = "hex_id"
  )



Mapping EHSA Results
This visualization highlights the spatial dynamics of bus trip activity over time. Red hexagons represent emerging hot spots, where clustering intensity is increasing, suggesting growing passenger activity. Blue hexagons indicate diminishing hot spots, where activity levels are decreasing over time. Grey areas show no statistically significant trend, meaning their Local Gi* values remain relatively stable.

tmap_mode("plot")

tm_shape(hex_ehsa) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "trend_type",
    fill.scale = tm_scale(values = c(
      "Emerging Hot Spot"     = "red",
      "Diminishing Hot Spot"  = "blue",
      "No Significant Trend"  = "grey80"
    )),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Emerging Hot Spot Trends")
  ) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








At the standard 95% confidence level, the Mann–Kendall test detected no statistically significant spatial trends across Singapore’s bus trip data. The resulting map shows all hexagons in grey, labelled as “No Significant Trend.” This suggests that with the current 3 month dataset, there is insufficient temporal variation for the test to identify any consistent upward or downward trend in trip intensity. This outcome is expected, as the Mann–Kendall test requires a reasonably long time series to establish monotonic changes.

alpha <- 0.10

gi_trend <- gi_trend %>%
  mutate(
    trend_sig   = !is.na(p_value) & p_value <= alpha,
    latest_sign = case_when(
      gi_latest >  0 ~ "hot",
      gi_latest <  0 ~ "cold",
      TRUE           ~ "neutral"
    ),
    ehsa_type = case_when(
      trend_sig & tau > 0  & latest_sign == "hot"  ~ "Emerging Hot Spot",
      trend_sig & tau < 0  & latest_sign == "hot"  ~ "Diminishing Hot Spot",
      trend_sig & tau < 0  & latest_sign == "cold" ~ "Emerging Cold Spot",
      trend_sig & tau > 0  & latest_sign == "cold" ~ "Diminishing Cold Spot",
      TRUE                                          ~ "No Significant Trend"
    )
  )

hex_ehsa <- hex_base %>%
  left_join(
    gi_trend %>% select(hex_id, ehsa_type, tau, p_value, gi_latest, gi_mean),
    by = "hex_id"
  )


tmap_mode("plot")

tm_shape(hex_ehsa) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "ehsa_type",
    fill.scale = tm_scale(values = c(
      "Emerging Hot Spot"     = "red",
      "Diminishing Hot Spot"  = "orange",
      "Emerging Cold Spot"    = "blue",
      "Diminishing Cold Spot" = "lightblue",
      "No Significant Trend"  = "grey80"
    )),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Emerging Hot Spot Analysis")
  ) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)








To further explore potential weak signals of change, the alpha level was relaxed to 0.10. However, even with this less stringent threshold, the spatial pattern remained unchanged as all hexagons were still classified as “No Significant Trend.” This reinforces the conclusion that the available three-month period does not provide enough temporal depth for meaningful detection of emerging or diminishing hot and cold spots. A longer observation window of 6 to 12 months would be needed to reveal significant spatial–temporal dynamics.

geocode <- function(block, streetname) {
  base_url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search"
  address <- paste(block, streetname, sep = " ")
  query <- list(
    "searchVal" = address,
    "returnGeom" = "Y",
    "getAddrDetails" = "N",
    "pageNum" = "1"
  )

  res <- GET(base_url, query = query)
  restext <- content(res, as = "text")

  output <- fromJSON(restext) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    select(results.LATITUDE, results.LONGITUDE)

  return(output)
}


HDBresale$LATITUDE <- 0
HDBresale$LONGITUDE <- 0

for (i in 1:nrow(HDBresale)){
  temp_output <- geocode(HDBresale[i,4],HDBresale[i,5])
  HDBresale$LATITUDE[i] <- temp_output$results.LATITUDE
  HDBresale$LONGITUDE[i] <- temp_output$results.LONGITUDE

Checking for overlapping data

Preparing the Data
For this in-class exercise, Hunan shapefile and Hunan_2012 data file will be used.
Using the steps you learned from previous hands-on, complete the following tasks:

import Hunan shapefile and parse it into a sf polygon feature object.
import Hunan_2012.csv file parse it into a tibble data.frame.
join Hunan and Hunan_2012 data.frames.


Importing Hunan shapefile

hunan_sf <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", 
                 layer = "Hunan")

  using driver `ESRI Shapefile'

Saving ACRA data

write_rds(acra_data,
          "data/rds/acra_data.rds")

Tidying ACRA data
select the target businesses by using SSIC code
derive the year and month fields from registration_incorporation_date field
tidy postal code values to avoid 5 digit
We need to confirm the postal code for those that are 5 digits. is the 0 supposed to be at the front or the back? we can confirm based on the address (street name).
56111 refers to restaurants SSIC code

biz_56111 <- acra_data%>%
  select(1:24) %>%
  filter(primary_ssic_code == 56111) %>%
  rename(date = registration_incorporation_date) %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date),
         YEAR = year(date),
         MONTH_NUM = month(date),
         MONTH_ABBR = month(date,
                            label = TRUE,
                            abbr = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(
    postal_code = str_pad(postal_code,
    width = 6, side = "left", pad = "0")) %>%
            filter(YEAR == 2025)

Geocoding
Extracting unique postal code from the postal_code field
*dont geocode too many. at max 5000 records*

postcodes <- unique(biz_56111$postal_code)

url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search"

found <- data.frame()
not_found <- data.frame(postcode = character())

for (pc in postcodes) {
  query <- list(
    searchVal = pc,
    returnGeom = "Y",
    getAddrDetails = "Y",
    pageNum = "1"
  )
  
  res <- GET(url, query = query)
  json <- content(res)
  
  if (json$found != 0) {
    df <- as.data.frame(json$results, stringAsFactors = FALSE)
    df$input_postcode <- pc
    found <- bind_rows(found, df)
  } else{
    not_found <- bind_rows(not_found, data.frame(postcode = pc))
  }
}

Appending the location information

biz_56111 = biz_56111 %>%
  left_join(found,
            by = c('postal_code' = 'POSTAL'))

converting into SF data frame

biz_56111_sf <- st_as_sf(biz_56111,
                         coords = c("X", "Y"),
                         crs=3414)


glimpse(biz_56111_sf)

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
This exercise shows how to model geographical accessibility in R using standard geospatial packages.
We will load, clean, and visualise spatial data, and calculate accessibility using several methods.

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Importing Geospatial Data
We start by reading the shapefiles using the sf package in R. Loading them as spatial objects allows us to use them in mapping and analysis. It is also a good practice to check that each file has been imported correctly and that its geometry type is properly recognised.

mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL")

Updating CRS Information

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Cleaning and Updating Attribute Fields
Next, we clean up the datasets by keeping only the necessary columns. We also create two additional fields to support our analysis. The first is capacity, which shows how much service an eldercare centre can provide. The second is demand, which reflects the level of need in each hexagon.

For this exercise, both values are set to 100 as placeholders. In a real-world project, they would be based on actual data such as population or service capacity.

eldercare <- eldercare %>%
  select(fid, ADDRESSPOS) %>%
  mutate(capacity = 100)

hexagons <- hexagons %>%
  select(fid) %>%
  mutate(demand = 100)

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Importing Distance Matrix
We load the OD matrix from a CSV file. Each record represents a pair of points: an origin (a hexagon) and a destination (an eldercare centre). The matrix includes the total travel distance between them, measured in metres. This gives us a full picture of how connected different parts of the study area are to eldercare services.

ODMatrix <- read_csv("data/aspatial/OD_Matrix.csv", skip = 0)

ODMatrix

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Tidying Distance Matrix
The imported data starts in a long format, meaning that each row shows one origin and one destination. For modelling, we need it in a wide format, where each row represents one origin and each column represents one destination. The value inside each cell shows the distance between them.

distmat <- ODMatrix %>%
  select(origin_id, destination_id, total_cost) %>%
  spread(destination_id, total_cost)%>%
  select(c(-c('origin_id')))

After restructuring, we convert the distances from metres to kilometres to make the numbers easier to interpret.

distmat_km <- as.matrix(distmat/1000)

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Computing Hansen’s Accessibility
We calculate accessibility using the SpatialAcc package. The function takes into account the demand, the capacity of eldercare centres, and the distance matrix. It produces an accessibility score for each hexagon. These scores are then joined back to the spatial grid so that they can be visualised on a map.

acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km, 
                            #d0 = 50,
                            power = 2, 
                            family = "Hansen"))
colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)
hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)

The default field name is very messy, we will rename it to accHansen by using the code chunk below.

colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
acc_Hansen

# A tibble: 3,125 × 1
   accHansen
       <dbl>
 1  1.65e-14
 2  1.10e-16
 3  3.87e-17
 4  1.48e-17
 5  1.05e-17
 6  5.08e-18
 7  1.77e-13
 8  9.98e-14
 9  5.67e-14
10  2.62e-14
# ℹ 3,115 more rows


Next, we will convert the data table into tibble format by using the code chunk below.

acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)

Lastly, bind_cols() of dplyr will be used to join the acc_Hansen tibble data frame with the hexagons simple feature data frame. The output is called hexagon_Hansen.

hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)
hexagon_Hansen

Actually, the steps above can be perform by using a single code chunk as shown below.

acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km, 
                            #d0 = 50,
                            power = 0.5, 
                            family = "Hansen"))

colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)
hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Visualising Hansen’s Accessibility

Extracting map extend
We then create a map to show the results. Each hexagon is shaded according to its accessibility score, where darker colours indicate better access to eldercare facilities. The eldercare centres are shown as red points on the same map. This visualisation helps us quickly see which parts of Singapore have good coverage and which areas may need more support.

mapex <- st_bbox(hexagons)

The code chunk below uses a collection of mapping fucntions of tmap package to create a high cartographic quality accessibility to eldercare centre in Singapore.

tm_shape(hexagon_Hansen,
         bbox = mapex) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "accHansen", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: Hansen method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Statistical Graphic Visualisation
To better understand the spatial patterns, we group the hexagons by URA Planning Region and compare their accessibility scores. A boxplot allows us to see which regions have higher or lower accessibility and how evenly access is distributed within each one.

hexagon_Hansen <- st_join(hexagon_Hansen, mpsz, 
                          join = st_intersects)

ggplot(data=hexagon_Hansen, 
       aes(y = log(accHansen), 
           x= REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat="summary", 
             fun.y="mean", 
             colour ="red", 
             size=2)

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Computing KD2SFCA’s Accessibility
We calculate accessibility again using this method. The main difference is that we define a catchment distance, such as 5km, which limits how far people are likely to travel for eldercare. This approach reflects real-world behaviour more realistically than a purely distance-based method.

acc_KD2SFCA <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km, 
                            d0 = 5,
                            power = 2, 
                            family = "KD2SFCA"))

colnames(acc_KD2SFCA) <- "accKD2SFCA"
acc_KD2SFCA <- as_tibble(acc_KD2SFCA)
hexagon_KD2SFCA <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_KD2SFCA)

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Visualising KD2SFCA’s Accessibility
After computing the scores, we display them on a map. The hexagons are shaded by their accessibility values, and darker areas show better access. The eldercare facilities are plotted again so that we can visually check how the accessibility patterns relate to their locations.

tm_shape(hexagon_KD2SFCA,
         bbox = mapex) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "accKD2SFCA", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: KD2SFCA method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Statistical Graphic Visualisation
We then compare the KD2SFCA results by region using boxplots. This helps reveal whether certain regions have more concentrated access to eldercare services while others may be underserved.

hexagon_KD2SFCA <- st_join(hexagon_KD2SFCA, mpsz, 
                          join = st_intersects)

ggplot(data=hexagon_KD2SFCA, 
       aes(y = accKD2SFCA, 
           x= REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat="summary", 
             fun.y="mean", 
             colour ="red", 
             size=2)

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Computing SAM Accessibility
We run the analysis again using the SAM method, setting a catchment distance and a power value for distance decay. The results give each hexagon an accessibility score that can be compared with those from the Hansen and KD2SFCA models.

acc_SAM <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                         eldercare$capacity,
                         distmat_km, 
                         d0 = 5,
                         power = 2, 
                         family = "SAM"))

colnames(acc_SAM) <- "accSAM"
acc_SAM <- as_tibble(acc_SAM)
hexagon_SAM <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_SAM)

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Visualising SAM’s Accessibility
We create another map to show the SAM results. As with the other methods, darker colours represent areas with better access to eldercare services. The eldercare centres are marked on top, making it easy to see how facility placement influences accessibility.

tm_shape(hexagon_SAM,
         bbox = mapex) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "accSAM", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: SAM method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)

title: Hands-on_Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Statistical Graphic Visualisation
Finally, we compare SAM accessibility scores across the different URA Planning Regions. The boxplots help identify which areas are performing well and which may require more attention. Together, the three models provide a comprehensive picture of how accessible eldercare services are across Singapore.

hexagon_SAM <- st_join(hexagon_SAM, mpsz, 
                       join = st_intersects)

ggplot(data=hexagon_SAM, 
       aes(y = accSAM, 
           x= REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat="summary", 
             fun.y="mean", 
             colour ="red", 
             size=2)

title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
A spatial technique for building hedonic pricing models that capture local variations in relationships between variables.
Unlike OLS, GWR considers spatial non-stationarity, showing how factors affect prices differently across locations.
Application: Condominium resale prices (2015) using structural and locational variables.




Two data sets will be used in this model building exercise, they are:

URA Master Plan subzone boundary in shapefile format (i.e. MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL)
condo_resale_2015 in csv format (i.e. condo_resale_2015.csv)

Installing and Loading the R packages

Packages Used



R package for building OLS and performing diagnostics tests

olsrr

R package for calibrating geographical weighted family of models

GWmodel

R package for multivariate data visualisation and analysis

corrplot

Spatial data handling

sf

Attribute data handling

tidyverse, especially readr, ggplot2 and dplyr

Choropleth mapping

tmap




The code chunk below uses p_load() of pacman package to check if the packages are installed in the computer. If they are, then they will be launched into R.

pacman::p_load(olsrr, corrplot, ggpubr, 
               sf, sfdep, GWmodel, tmap, 
               tidyverse, gtsummary,
               performance, RColorBrewer)











Note



The GWmodel package offers a range of spatial analysis tools that focus on localized data. These include geographically weighted (GW) summary statistics, principal component analysis, discriminant analysis, and different types of GW regression. Some of these methods also come in robust versions that can handle outliers.
Typically, the results or parameters produced by GWmodel are visualized as maps, making it a powerful tool for exploring spatial patterns. This exploratory step often helps guide and refine more detailed or advanced statistical analyses that follow.

title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
Importing geospatial data
The geospatial data used in this hands-on exercise is called MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL. It is in ESRI shapefile format. The shapefile consists of URA Master Plan 2014’s planning subzone boundaries. Polygon features are used to represent these geographic boundaries. The GIS data is in svy21 projected coordinates systems.
The code chunk below is used to import MP_SUBZONE_WEB_PL shapefile by using st_read() of sf packages.

mpsz = st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", 
               layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL")

section: Converting aspatial data frame into a sf object

Converting aspatial data frame into a sf object
The condo_resale tibble data frame is aspatial. We will convert it to a sf object. The code chunk below converts condo_resale data frame into a simple feature data frame by using st_as_sf() of sf.

condo_resale.sf <- st_as_sf(condo_resale,
                            coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"),
                            crs=4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs=3414)

title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
EDA using statistical graphics
We can plot the distribution of SELLING_PRICE by using appropriate Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) as shown in the code chunk below.

ggplot(data=condo_resale.sf, 
       aes(x=`SELLING_PRICE`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")








The figure above reveals a right skewed distribution. This means that more condominium units were transacted at relative lower prices.
Statistically, the skewed dsitribution can be normalised by using log transformation. The code chunk below is used to derive a new variable called LOG_SELLING_PRICE by using a log transformation on the variable SELLING_PRICE. It is performed using mutate() of dplyr package.

condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf %>%
  mutate(`LOG_SELLING_PRICE` = log(SELLING_PRICE))

Now, you can plot the LOG_SELLING_PRICE using the code chunk below.

ggplot(data=condo_resale.sf, 
       aes(x=`LOG_SELLING_PRICE`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")








Notice that the distribution is relatively less skewed after the transformation.

title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
Drawing Statistical Point Map
Lastly, we want to reveal the geospatial distribution condominium resale prices in Singapore. The map will be prepared by using tmap package.
First, we will turn on the interactive mode of tmap by using the code chunk below.

tmap_mode("plot")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"
ℹ toggle with `tmap::ttm()`


Next, the code chunks below is used to create an interactive point symbol map.

tm_shape(mpsz_svy21)+
  tm_polygons() +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +  
  tm_dots(fill = "SELLING_PRICE",
          fill_alpha = 0.6,
          size = 0.5,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style="quantile")) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(11,14))








Notice that tm_dots() is used instead of tm_bubbles().
set_zoom_limits argument of tm_view() sets the minimum and maximum zoom level to 11 and 14 respectively.
Before moving on to the next section, the code below will be used to turn R display into plot mode.

tmap_mode("plot")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"

title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
Simple Linear Regression Method
First, we will build a simple linear regression model by using SELLING_PRICE as the dependent variable and AREA_SQM as the independent variable.

condo.slr <- lm(formula=SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM, 
                data = condo_resale.sf)

lm() returns an object of class “lm” or for multiple responses of class c(“mlm”, “lm”).
The functions summary() and anova() can be used to obtain and print a summary and analysis of variance table of the results. The generic accessor functions coefficients, effects, fitted values and residuals extract various useful features of the value returned by lm.

summary(condo.slr)

The regression equation is y = -258121.1 + 14719x₁, meaning that SELLING_PRICE increases by about 14,719 for each unit increase in AREA_SQM.
R² = 0.4518, indicating the model explains about 45% of the variance in resale prices.
The p-value (< 0.0001) shows the model is statistically significant, so we reject the null hypothesis that the mean alone predicts prices well.

Multiple Linear Regression Method

Visualising the relationships of the independent variables

Before building a multiple regression model, it is essential to confirm that independent variables are not highly correlated.
High correlation among predictors can distort model accuracy, a problem known as multicollinearity.
A correlation matrix helps visualize relationships between variables.
In this exercise, the corrplot package (and pairs() in R) is used to plot a scatterplot matrix showing correlations among independent variables in condo_resale.


corrplot(cor(condo_resale[, 5:23]), 
         diag = FALSE, 
         order = "AOE",
         tl.pos = "td", 
         tl.cex = 0.5, 
         method = "number", 
         type = "upper")








Matrix reorder is very important for mining the hidden structure and patter in the matrix. There are four methods in corrplot (parameter order), named “AOE”, “FPC”, “hclust”, “alphabet”. In the code chunk above, AOE order is used.
From the scatterplot matrix, it is clear that Freehold is highly correlated to LEASE_99YEAR. In view of this, it is wiser to only include either one of them in the subsequent model building. As a result, LEASE_99YEAR is excluded in the subsequent model building.

title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
Regression Diagnostics
Regression diagnostics are methods used to check whether a regression model meets its assumptions and how well it fits the data. They help identify problems such as non-linear patterns, errors that are not normally distributed, unequal variance or data points that strongly affect the results. These checks ensure that the model’s findings are accurate and reliable.
The olsrr R package provides tools for performing OLS regression diagnostics:

comprehensive regression output
residual diagnostics
measures of influence
heteroskedasticity tests
collinearity diagnostics
model fit assessment
variable contribution assessment
variable selection procedures


Multicollinearity test
Multicollinearity happens when two or more independent variables in a model are closely related. When this occurs, a change in one variable is linked to a change in another, making it hard for the model to separate their individual effects on the outcome.
Testing for multicollinearity is important in multiple linear regression because it affects how reliable and clear the model’s results are. When variables are highly correlated, the estimated coefficients can become unstable and difficult to interpret. This can cause misleading results, such as making a variable seem unimportant when it actually has a real effect.
In the code chunk below, the check_collinearity() of performance package is used to test if there are sign of multicollinearity.

check_collinearity(condo.mlr1)

# Check for Multicollinearity

Low Correlation

                 Term  VIF   VIF 95% CI adj. VIF Tolerance Tolerance 95% CI
             AREA_SQM 1.15 [1.09, 1.23]     1.07      0.87     [0.81, 0.92]
                  AGE 1.41 [1.33, 1.52]     1.19      0.71     [0.66, 0.75]
             PROX_CBD 1.57 [1.47, 1.69]     1.25      0.64     [0.59, 0.68]
       PROX_CHILDCARE 3.26 [3.00, 3.56]     1.81      0.31     [0.28, 0.33]
             PROX_MRT 1.91 [1.78, 2.07]     1.38      0.52     [0.48, 0.56]

            PROX_PARK 1.21 [1.15, 1.29]     1.10      0.83     [0.77, 0.87]
     PROX_PRIMARY_SCH 2.21 [2.05, 2.40]     1.49      0.45     [0.42, 0.49]

        PROX_BUS_STOP 2.85 [2.62, 3.10]     1.69      0.35     [0.32, 0.38]

mlr.vif <- check_collinearity(condo.mlr1)
plot(mlr.vif)








Since the VIF of the independent variables are less than 10. We can safely conclude that there are no sign of multicollinearity among the independent variables.


Test for Non-Linearity
In multiple linear regression, it is important for us to test the assumption that linearity and additivity of the relationship between dependent and independent variables.
In the code chunk below, the ols_plot_resid_fit() of olsrr package is used to perform linearity assumption test.

check_model(condo.mlr1,
            check = "linearity")








The figure above reveals that most of the data points are scattered around the 0 line, hence we can safely conclude that the relationships between the dependent variable and independent variables are linear.


Test for Normality Assumption
The normality assumption test for multiple linear regression checks if the model’s residuals (the differences between observed and predicted values) are normally distributed. This is crucial for accurate hypothesis testing and confidence intervals. To test this, you can use visual methods like histograms and Q-Q plots of the residuals, or conduct statistical tests like Shapiro-Wilk test and Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
In the code chunk below, check_normality() of performance package is used to perform normality assumption test on condo.mlr1 model.

check_normality(condo.mlr1)

Warning: Non-normality of residuals detected (p < .001).


The print above reveals that the p-value of the normality assumption test is less than alpha value of 0.05. Hence we reject the normality assumption at 95% confident level.







Note




check_normality() calls stats::shapiro.test and checks the standardized residuals (or studentized residuals for mixed models) for normal distribution.
Note that this formal test almost always yields significant results for the distribution of residuals and visual inspection (e.g. Q-Q plots) are preferable.




Instead of showing the test statistic, plot() of see package can be used to plot the output of check_normality() for visual inspection as shown below.

plot(check_normality(condo.mlr1), 
     type = "qq")

For confidence bands, please install `qqplotr`.









Q-Q plot above below shows that majority of the data points are felt along the zero line.
Another way to check for normality assumption visual is by using check_model() of performance package as shown in the code chunk below.

check_model(condo.mlr1,
            check= "normality")








The figure reveals that the residual of the multiple linear regression model
(i.e. condo.mlr1) resembles normal distribution.


Testing for Spatial Autocorrelation
The hedonic model we try to build are using geographically referenced data. Hence, it is crucial to check for spatial autocorrelation because its presence can produce unreliable and misleading results. Traditional regression models, such as ordinary least squares (OLS), assume that observations are independent of one another. However, spatial data often violates this assumption.
Spatial autocorrelation is the correlation of a variable with itself across different spatial locations. Positive spatial autocorrelation means nearby features tend to be more similar, while negative autocorrelation means they tend to be more dissimilar. This phenomenon is based on the first law of geography: “Everything is related to everything else, but nearby things are more related than distant things”.
Ignoring spatial autocorrelation in a regression model can lead to serious statistical issues:

Biased and inefficient coefficient estimates: If autocorrelation is present, standard errors of the model coefficients can be wrong, leading to unreliable hypothesis tests (p-values). The model might appear more significant than it is.
Misleading significance tests: Standard regression models cannot distinguish between true explanatory power and the influence of spatial patterns, resulting in inaccurate p-values.
Model misspecification: Significant spatial autocorrelation in the regression residuals often signals that important explanatory variables are missing from the model. The spatial patterning of the residuals (over- and under-predictions) can provide clues about what these missing variables might be.
Inflated Type I error rates: Researchers might incorrectly reject a true null.

To test for spatial autocorrelation, We can run a Moran’s I test on the model’s residuals. Significant spatial autocorrelation in the residuals means the model is not capturing the full spatial story.
In order to perform spatial autocorrelation test, we need to export the residual of the hedonic pricing model and save it as a data frame first.

mlr.output <- as.data.frame(condo.mlr1$residuals)

Next, we will join the newly created data frame with condo_resale.sf object.

condo_resale.sf <- cbind(condo_resale.sf, 
                        condo.mlr1$residuals) %>%
rename(`MLR_RES` = `condo.mlr1.residuals`)

Next, we will use tmap package to display the distribution of the residuals on an interactive map.
The code churn below will turn on the interactive mode of tmap.

tmap_mode("plot")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"


The code chunks below is used to create an interactive point symbol map.

tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill_alpha = 0.4) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +  
  tm_dots(
    fill = "MLR_RES",
    size = 0.7,
    col = "black",
    fill.scale = tm_scale(
      n = 10,
      values = rev(
        brewer.pal(11, "RdBu")),
      style = "quantile",
      midpoint = NA),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residuals")
  ) + 
  tm_title("LM Residuals (Quantile Classification)") +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(11,14))








Remember to switch back to “plot” mode before continue.

tmap_mode("plot")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"


The figure above reveal that there is sign of spatial autocorrelation.
To proof that our observation is indeed true, Global Moran’s I test will be performed
First, we will compute the distance-based weight matrix by using st_dist_band() function of sfdep.

condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf %>% 
  mutate(
    nb = st_dist_band(
      st_geometry(geometry), 
                 upper = 1500),
    wt = st_weights(
      nb, style = "W"),
    .before = 1) 

Warning: There was 1 warning in `stopifnot()`.
ℹ In argument: `nb = st_dist_band(st_geometry(geometry), upper = 1500)`.
Caused by warning in `spdep::dnearneigh()`:
! neighbour object has 10 sub-graphs


Next, global_moran_perm() of sfdep package will be used to perform Moran’s I test for residual spatial autocorrelation

set.seed(1234)
global_moran_perm(
  condo_resale.sf$MLR_RES, 
  nb = condo_resale.sf$nb, 
  wt = condo_resale.sf$wt,
  alternative = "two.sided", 
  nsim = 499)


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  x 
weights: listw  
number of simulations + 1: 500 

statistic = 0.14389, observed rank = 500, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided


The Global Moran’s I test for residual spatial autocorrelation shows that it’s p-value is less than 0.00000000000000022 which is less than the alpha value of 0.05. Hence, we will reject the null hypothesis that the residuals are randomly distributed.
Since the Observed Global Moran I = 0.14389 which is greater than 0, we can infer than the residuals resemble cluster distribution.

title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
Building Fixed Bandwidth GWR Model

Computing fixed bandwith
In the code chunk below bw.gwr() of GWModel is used to determine the optimal fixed bandwidth to use in the model. Notice that the argument adaptive is set to FALSE indicates that we are interested to compute the fixed bandwidth.
There are two possible approaches can be used to determine the stopping rule, they are CV cross-validation approach and AIC corrected (AICc) approach. We define the stopping rule using approach agreement.

bw.fixed <- bw.gwr(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE  + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE    +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + 
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL   + 
    PROX_BUS_STOP   + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + 
    FREEHOLD, 
  data=condo_resale.sf, 
  approach="CV", 
  kernel="gaussian", 
  adaptive=FALSE,

The result shows that the recommended bandwidth is 971.3405 metres.






Note



The bandwidth value is expressed in metres because the spatial dataset adopts Singapore’s standard coordinate reference system, SVY21 (EPSG:3414), which measures all spatial distances and areas in metres. When the Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) function is executed with the parameters adaptive equals false and longlat equals false, the model treats the data as being in a projected planar coordinate system. Consequently, the bandwidth produced represents a fixed distance measured in metres. In this case, the recommended bandwidth of approximately 971 metres indicates that the model considers nearby data points within roughly a one-kilometre radius when estimating local spatial relationships. If the dataset were instead based on a geographic coordinate system using latitude and longitude, and the longlat parameter was set to true, the bandwidth would have been expressed in degrees.




GWModel method - fixed bandwith
Now we can use the code chunk below to calibrate the gwr model using fixed bandwidth and gaussian kernel.

  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE  + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE    +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL   + 
    PROX_BUS_STOP   + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + 
    FREEHOLD, 
  data=condo_resale.sf, 
  bw=bw.fixed, 
  kernel = 'gaussian', 
  longlat = FALSE)

title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
Visualising GWR Output
Besides the regression residuals, the output table also includes several important fields. These include the observed and predicted y values, the condition number, the local R² values, the residuals and the coefficients and standard errors for the explanatory variables.

Condition Number: This value checks for local multicollinearity, which happens when variables are too closely related. A condition number above 30 suggests the results may be unstable or unreliable.
Local R²: Shows how well the model fits the observed data in each area. Values closer to 1 mean a better fit, while low values mean the model performs poorly.
Predicted Values: These are the estimated values produced by the model based on the input variables.
Residuals: Shows the difference between the observed and predicted values. Standardized residuals make comparison easier and can be mapped to show areas of under or overprediction.
Coefficient Standard Errors: Measures how reliable each coefficient is. Smaller values mean higher confidence, while large ones may indicate local multicollinearity problems.

They are all stored in a SpatialPointsDataFrame or SpatialPolygonsDataFrame object integrated with fit.points, GWR coefficient estimates, y value, predicted values, coefficient standard errors and t-values in its “data” slot in an object called SDF of the output list.

title: Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA) focus on the relationships between each observation and its surroundings, rather than providing a single summary of these relationships across the map. In this sense, they are not summary statistics but scores that allow us to learn more about the spatial structure in our data. To simplify, they break things down to the individual location level. They show where clustering or outliers exist in the study area.
The general intuition behind the metrics however is similar to that of global ones. Some of them are even mathematically connected, where the global version can be decomposed into a collection of local ones. One such example are Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA). Beside LISA, Getis-Ord’s Gi-statistics will be introduce as an alternative LMSA statistics that present complementary information or allow us to obtain similar insights for geographically referenced data.
In this hands-on exercise, we will learn how to compute Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA) by using sfdep package. By the end to this hands-on exercise, you will be able to:

import geospatial data using appropriate function(s) of sf package
import csv file using appropriate function of readr package,
perform relational join using appropriate join function of dplyr package,
compute Local Indicator of Spatial Association (LISA) statistics for detecting clusters and outliers by using appropriate functions sfdep package;
compute Getis-Ord’s Gi-statistics for detecting hot spot or/and cold spot area by using appropriate functions of sfdep package; and
to visualise the analysis output by using tmap package

text:
Performing relational join
After the importing of the files into the R environment, we will proceed to join the files.
The code chunk below will be used to update the attribute table of hunan’s SpatialPolygonsDataFrame with the attribute fields of hunan2012 dataframe. This is performed by using left_join() of dplyr package.

hunan <- left_join(hunan,hunan2012) %>%
  select(1:4, 7, 15)

title: Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Computing Contiguity Spatial Weights
Before we can compute the local spatial autocorrelation statistics like Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (GMSA), we need to construct a spatial weights of the study area. The spatial weights is used to define the neighbourhood relationships between the geographical units (i.e. county) in the study area.
In the code chunk below, st_contiguity() of sfdep package is used to compute contiguity weight matrices for the study area. This function builds a neighbours list based on regions with contiguous boundaries. If you look at the documentation you will see that you can pass a “queen” argument that takes TRUE or FALSE as options. If you do not specify this argument the default is set to TRUE, that is, if you don’t specify queen = FALSE this function will return a list of first order neighbours using the Queen criteria.
Next, st_weights() is used to calculate polygon spatial weights from the nb list.
st_weights() provides three arguments, they are:

nb: A neighbor list object as created by st_neighbors().
style: Default “W” for row standardized weights. This value can also be “B”, “C”, “U”, “minmax”, and “S”. B is the basic binary coding, W is row standardised (sums over all links to n), C is globally standardised (sums over all links to n), U is equal to C divided by the number of neighbours (sums over all links to unity), while S is the variance-stabilizing coding scheme proposed by Tiefelsdorf et al. 1999, p. 167-168 (sums over all links to n).
allow_zero: If TRUE, assigns zero as lagged value to zone without neighbors.


wm_q <- hunan %>%
  mutate(nb = st_contiguity(geometry),
         wt = st_weights(
           nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)
