title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
EDA using statistical graphics
We can plot the distribution of SELLING_PRICE by using appropriate Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) as shown in the code chunk below.

ggplot(data=condo_resale.sf, 
       aes(x=`SELLING_PRICE`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")








The figure above reveals a right skewed distribution. This means that more condominium units were transacted at relative lower prices.
Statistically, the skewed dsitribution can be normalised by using log transformation. The code chunk below is used to derive a new variable called LOG_SELLING_PRICE by using a log transformation on the variable SELLING_PRICE. It is performed using mutate() of dplyr package.

condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf %>%
  mutate(`LOG_SELLING_PRICE` = log(SELLING_PRICE))

Now, you can plot the LOG_SELLING_PRICE using the code chunk below.

ggplot(data=condo_resale.sf, 
       aes(x=`LOG_SELLING_PRICE`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")








Notice that the distribution is relatively less skewed after the transformation.

title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
Drawing Statistical Point Map
Lastly, we want to reveal the geospatial distribution condominium resale prices in Singapore. The map will be prepared by using tmap package.
First, we will turn on the interactive mode of tmap by using the code chunk below.

tmap_mode("plot")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"
ℹ toggle with `tmap::ttm()`


Next, the code chunks below is used to create an interactive point symbol map.

tm_shape(mpsz_svy21)+
  tm_polygons() +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +  
  tm_dots(fill = "SELLING_PRICE",
          fill_alpha = 0.6,
          size = 0.5,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style="quantile")) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(11,14))








Notice that tm_dots() is used instead of tm_bubbles().
set_zoom_limits argument of tm_view() sets the minimum and maximum zoom level to 11 and 14 respectively.
Before moving on to the next section, the code below will be used to turn R display into plot mode.

tmap_mode("plot")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"

title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
Simple Linear Regression Method
First, we will build a simple linear regression model by using SELLING_PRICE as the dependent variable and AREA_SQM as the independent variable.

condo.slr <- lm(formula=SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM, 
                data = condo_resale.sf)

lm() returns an object of class “lm” or for multiple responses of class c(“mlm”, “lm”).
The functions summary() and anova() can be used to obtain and print a summary and analysis of variance table of the results. The generic accessor functions coefficients, effects, fitted values and residuals extract various useful features of the value returned by lm.

summary(condo.slr)


Call:
lm(formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM, data = condo_resale.sf)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-3695815  -391764   -87517   258900 13503875 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -258121.1    63517.2  -4.064 5.09e-05 ***
AREA_SQM      14719.0      428.1  34.381  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 942700 on 1434 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4518,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.4515 
F-statistic:  1182 on 1 and 1434 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16



The regression equation is y = -258121.1 + 14719x₁, meaning that SELLING_PRICE increases by about 14,719 for each unit increase in AREA_SQM.
R² = 0.4518, indicating the model explains about 45% of the variance in resale prices.
The p-value (< 0.0001) shows the model is statistically significant, so we reject the null hypothesis that the mean alone predicts prices well.
Both Intercept (B₀) and AREA_SQM (B₁) have p-values < 0.001, confirming they are significant predictors.
The best-fit line can be visualized in a scatterplot using geom_smooth(method = “lm”) in ggplot2.


ggplot(data=condo_resale.sf,  
       aes(x=`AREA_SQM`, y=`SELLING_PRICE`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









Figure above reveals that there are a few statistical outliers with relatively high selling prices.

title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
Multiple Linear Regression Method

Visualising the relationships of the independent variables

Before building a multiple regression model, it is essential to confirm that independent variables are not highly correlated.
High correlation among predictors can distort model accuracy, a problem known as multicollinearity.
A correlation matrix helps visualize relationships between variables.
In this exercise, the corrplot package (and pairs() in R) is used to plot a scatterplot matrix showing correlations among independent variables in condo_resale.


corrplot(cor(condo_resale[, 5:23]), 
         diag = FALSE, 
         order = "AOE",
         tl.pos = "td", 
         tl.cex = 0.5, 
         method = "number", 
         type = "upper")








Matrix reorder is very important for mining the hidden structure and patter in the matrix. There are four methods in corrplot (parameter order), named “AOE”, “FPC”, “hclust”, “alphabet”. In the code chunk above, AOE order is used.
From the scatterplot matrix, it is clear that Freehold is highly correlated to LEASE_99YEAR. In view of this, it is wiser to only include either one of them in the subsequent model building. As a result, LEASE_99YEAR is excluded in the subsequent model building.

section: Building a hedonic pricing model using multiple linear regression method
text:
Building a hedonic pricing model using multiple linear regression method
The code chunk below using lm() to calibrate the multiple linear regression model.

condo.mlr <- lm(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE  + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_HAWKER_MARKET   +
    PROX_KINDERGARTEN   + PROX_MRT  + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH +
    PROX_SHOPPING_MALL  + PROX_SUPERMARKET + 
    PROX_BUS_STOP   + NO_Of_UNITS + 
    FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD, 
  data=condo_resale.sf)
summary(condo.mlr)

title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
Regression Diagnostics
Regression diagnostics are methods used to check whether a regression model meets its assumptions and how well it fits the data. They help identify problems such as non-linear patterns, errors that are not normally distributed, unequal variance or data points that strongly affect the results. These checks ensure that the model’s findings are accurate and reliable.
The olsrr R package provides tools for performing OLS regression diagnostics:

comprehensive regression output
residual diagnostics
measures of influence
heteroskedasticity tests
collinearity diagnostics
model fit assessment
variable contribution assessment
variable selection procedures


Multicollinearity test
Multicollinearity happens when two or more independent variables in a model are closely related. When this occurs, a change in one variable is linked to a change in another, making it hard for the model to separate their individual effects on the outcome.
Testing for multicollinearity is important in multiple linear regression because it affects how reliable and clear the model’s results are. When variables are highly correlated, the estimated coefficients can become unstable and difficult to interpret. This can cause misleading results, such as making a variable seem unimportant when it actually has a real effect.
In the code chunk below, the check_collinearity() of performance package is used to test if there are sign of multicollinearity.

check_collinearity(condo.mlr1)

# Check for Multicollinearity

Low Correlation

             PROX_CBD 1.57 [1.47, 1.69]     1.25      0.64     [0.59, 0.68]
       PROX_CHILDCARE 3.26 [3.00, 3.56]     1.81      0.31     [0.28, 0.33]

mlr.vif <- check_collinearity(condo.mlr1)
plot(mlr.vif)








Since the VIF of the independent variables are less than 10. We can safely conclude that there are no sign of multicollinearity among the independent variables.


Test for Non-Linearity
In multiple linear regression, it is important for us to test the assumption that linearity and additivity of the relationship between dependent and independent variables.
In the code chunk below, the ols_plot_resid_fit() of olsrr package is used to perform linearity assumption test.

check_model(condo.mlr1,
            check = "linearity")








The figure above reveals that most of the data points are scattered around the 0 line, hence we can safely conclude that the relationships between the dependent variable and independent variables are linear.


Test for Normality Assumption
The normality assumption test for multiple linear regression checks if the model’s residuals (the differences between observed and predicted values) are normally distributed. This is crucial for accurate hypothesis testing and confidence intervals. To test this, you can use visual methods like histograms and Q-Q plots of the residuals, or conduct statistical tests like Shapiro-Wilk test and Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
In the code chunk below, check_normality() of performance package is used to perform normality assumption test on condo.mlr1 model.

check_normality(condo.mlr1)

Warning: Non-normality of residuals detected (p < .001).


The print above reveals that the p-value of the normality assumption test is less than alpha value of 0.05. Hence we reject the normality assumption at 95% confident level.







Note




check_normality() calls stats::shapiro.test and checks the standardized residuals (or studentized residuals for mixed models) for normal distribution.
Note that this formal test almost always yields significant results for the distribution of residuals and visual inspection (e.g. Q-Q plots) are preferable.




Instead of showing the test statistic, plot() of see package can be used to plot the output of check_normality() for visual inspection as shown below.

plot(check_normality(condo.mlr1), 
     type = "qq")

For confidence bands, please install `qqplotr`.









Q-Q plot above below shows that majority of the data points are felt along the zero line.
Another way to check for normality assumption visual is by using check_model() of performance package as shown in the code chunk below.

check_model(condo.mlr1,
            check= "normality")








The figure reveals that the residual of the multiple linear regression model
(i.e. condo.mlr1) resembles normal distribution.


Testing for Spatial Autocorrelation
The hedonic model we try to build are using geographically referenced data. Hence, it is crucial to check for spatial autocorrelation because its presence can produce unreliable and misleading results. Traditional regression models, such as ordinary least squares (OLS), assume that observations are independent of one another. However, spatial data often violates this assumption.
Spatial autocorrelation is the correlation of a variable with itself across different spatial locations. Positive spatial autocorrelation means nearby features tend to be more similar, while negative autocorrelation means they tend to be more dissimilar. This phenomenon is based on the first law of geography: “Everything is related to everything else, but nearby things are more related than distant things”.
Ignoring spatial autocorrelation in a regression model can lead to serious statistical issues:

Biased and inefficient coefficient estimates: If autocorrelation is present, standard errors of the model coefficients can be wrong, leading to unreliable hypothesis tests (p-values). The model might appear more significant than it is.
Misleading significance tests: Standard regression models cannot distinguish between true explanatory power and the influence of spatial patterns, resulting in inaccurate p-values.
Model misspecification: Significant spatial autocorrelation in the regression residuals often signals that important explanatory variables are missing from the model. The spatial patterning of the residuals (over- and under-predictions) can provide clues about what these missing variables might be.
Inflated Type I error rates: Researchers might incorrectly reject a true null.

To test for spatial autocorrelation, We can run a Moran’s I test on the model’s residuals. Significant spatial autocorrelation in the residuals means the model is not capturing the full spatial story.
In order to perform spatial autocorrelation test, we need to export the residual of the hedonic pricing model and save it as a data frame first.

mlr.output <- as.data.frame(condo.mlr1$residuals)

Next, we will join the newly created data frame with condo_resale.sf object.

condo_resale.sf <- cbind(condo_resale.sf, 
                        condo.mlr1$residuals) %>%
rename(`MLR_RES` = `condo.mlr1.residuals`)

Next, we will use tmap package to display the distribution of the residuals on an interactive map.
The code churn below will turn on the interactive mode of tmap.

tmap_mode("plot")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"


The code chunks below is used to create an interactive point symbol map.

tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill_alpha = 0.4) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +  
  tm_dots(
    fill = "MLR_RES",
    size = 0.7,
    col = "black",
    fill.scale = tm_scale(
      n = 10,
      values = rev(
        brewer.pal(11, "RdBu")),
      style = "quantile",
      midpoint = NA),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residuals")
  ) + 
  tm_title("LM Residuals (Quantile Classification)") +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(11,14))








Remember to switch back to “plot” mode before continue.

tmap_mode("plot")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"


The figure above reveal that there is sign of spatial autocorrelation.
To proof that our observation is indeed true, Global Moran’s I test will be performed
First, we will compute the distance-based weight matrix by using st_dist_band() function of sfdep.

condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf %>% 
  mutate(
    nb = st_dist_band(
      st_geometry(geometry), 
                 upper = 1500),
    wt = st_weights(
      nb, style = "W"),
    .before = 1) 

Warning: There was 1 warning in `stopifnot()`.
ℹ In argument: `nb = st_dist_band(st_geometry(geometry), upper = 1500)`.
Caused by warning in `spdep::dnearneigh()`:
! neighbour object has 10 sub-graphs


Next, global_moran_perm() of sfdep package will be used to perform Moran’s I test for residual spatial autocorrelation

set.seed(1234)
global_moran_perm(
  condo_resale.sf$MLR_RES, 
  nb = condo_resale.sf$nb, 
  wt = condo_resale.sf$wt,
  alternative = "two.sided", 
  nsim = 499)


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  x 
weights: listw  
number of simulations + 1: 500 

statistic = 0.14389, observed rank = 500, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided


The Global Moran’s I test for residual spatial autocorrelation shows that it’s p-value is less than 0.00000000000000022 which is less than the alpha value of 0.05. Hence, we will reject the null hypothesis that the residuals are randomly distributed.
Since the Observed Global Moran I = 0.14389 which is greater than 0, we can infer than the residuals resemble cluster distribution.

Building Fixed Bandwidth GWR Model

Computing fixed bandwith
In the code chunk below bw.gwr() of GWModel is used to determine the optimal fixed bandwidth to use in the model. Notice that the argument adaptive is set to FALSE indicates that we are interested to compute the fixed bandwidth.
There are two possible approaches can be used to determine the stopping rule, they are CV cross-validation approach and AIC corrected (AICc) approach. We define the stopping rule using approach agreement.

bw.fixed <- bw.gwr(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE  + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE    +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + 
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL   + 
    PROX_BUS_STOP   + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + 
    FREEHOLD, 
  data=condo_resale.sf, 
  approach="CV", 
  kernel="gaussian", 
  adaptive=FALSE, 
  longlat=FALSE)

The result shows that the recommended bandwidth is 971.3405 metres.






Note



The bandwidth value is expressed in metres because the spatial dataset adopts Singapore’s standard coordinate reference system, SVY21 (EPSG:3414), which measures all spatial distances and areas in metres. When the Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) function is executed with the parameters adaptive equals false and longlat equals false, the model treats the data as being in a projected planar coordinate system. Consequently, the bandwidth produced represents a fixed distance measured in metres. In this case, the recommended bandwidth of approximately 971 metres indicates that the model considers nearby data points within roughly a one-kilometre radius when estimating local spatial relationships. If the dataset were instead based on a geographic coordinate system using latitude and longitude, and the longlat parameter was set to true, the bandwidth would have been expressed in degrees.




GWModel method - fixed bandwith
Now we can use the code chunk below to calibrate the gwr model using fixed bandwidth and gaussian kernel.

gwr.fixed <- gwr.basic(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE  + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE    +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL   + 
    PROX_BUS_STOP   + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + 
    FREEHOLD, 
  data=condo_resale.sf, 
  bw=bw.fixed, 
  kernel = 'gaussian', 
  longlat = FALSE)

title: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
text:
Visualising GWR Output
Besides the regression residuals, the output table also includes several important fields. These include the observed and predicted y values, the condition number, the local R² values, the residuals and the coefficients and standard errors for the explanatory variables.

Condition Number: This value checks for local multicollinearity, which happens when variables are too closely related. A condition number above 30 suggests the results may be unstable or unreliable.
Local R²: Shows how well the model fits the observed data in each area. Values closer to 1 mean a better fit, while low values mean the model performs poorly.
Predicted Values: These are the estimated values produced by the model based on the input variables.
Residuals: Shows the difference between the observed and predicted values. Standardized residuals make comparison easier and can be mapped to show areas of under or overprediction.
Coefficient Standard Errors: Measures how reliable each coefficient is. Smaller values mean higher confidence, while large ones may indicate local multicollinearity problems.

They are all stored in a SpatialPointsDataFrame or SpatialPolygonsDataFrame object integrated with fit.points, GWR coefficient estimates, y value, predicted values, coefficient standard errors and t-values in its “data” slot in an object called SDF of the output list.

title: In-class Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
This exercise shows how to model geographical accessibility in R using standard geospatial packages.
We will load, clean, and visualise spatial data, and calculate accessibility using several methods.

title: In-class Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Cleaning and Updating Attribute Fields
Next, we clean up the datasets by keeping only the necessary columns. We also create two additional fields to support our analysis. The first is capacity, which shows how much service an eldercare centre can provide. The second is demand, which reflects the level of need in each hexagon.

For this exercise, both values are set to 100 as placeholders. In a real-world project, they would be based on actual data such as population or service capacity.

eldercare <- eldercare %>%
  select(fid, ADDRESSPOS) %>%
  mutate(capacity = 100)

hexagons <- hexagons %>%
  select(fid) %>%
  mutate(demand = 100)

title: In-class Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Importing Distance Matrix
We load the OD matrix from a CSV file. Each record represents a pair of points: an origin (a hexagon) and a destination (an eldercare centre). The matrix includes the total travel distance between them, measured in metres. This gives us a full picture of how connected different parts of the study area are to eldercare services.

ODMatrix <- read_csv("data/aspatial/OD_Matrix.csv", skip = 0)

title: In-class Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Tidying Distance Matrix
The imported data starts in a long format, meaning that each row shows one origin and one destination. For modelling, we need it in a wide format, where each row represents one origin and each column represents one destination. The value inside each cell shows the distance between them.

distmat <- ODMatrix %>%
  select(origin_id, destination_id, total_cost) %>%
  spread(destination_id, total_cost)%>%
  select(c(-c('origin_id')))

After restructuring, we convert the distances from metres to kilometres to make the numbers easier to interpret.

distmat_km <- as.matrix(distmat/1000)

title: In-class Ex09 - Modelling Geographical Accessibility
text:
Computing Hansen’s Accessibility
We calculate accessibility using the SpatialAcc package. The function takes into account the demand, the capacity of eldercare centres, and the distance matrix. It produces an accessibility score for each hexagon. These scores are then joined back to the spatial grid so that they can be visualised on a map.

acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km, 
                            #d0 = 50,
                            power = 2, 
                            family = "Hansen"))
colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)
hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Good
text:
The locations of businesses and firms are central to urban development, influencing economic growth, job creation, and the availability of resources and services for residents and other businesses. Strategic locations provide competitive advantages, access to talent and infrastructure, and impact brand image and market positioning, while also shaping the city’s overall character and functionality by fostering specialized districts and facilitating efficient supply chains and employee commutes.
Studying the spatio-temporal patterns of businesses and firms is crucial for urban development because it reveals how economic activity and urban forms evolve, enabling better urban planning, promoting sustainability, identifying urban inefficiencies, and enhancing quality of life. By understanding where and when businesses locate and operate, urban planners can design cities more effectively, anticipate growth, ensure resource efficiency, and tailor infrastructure to support economic vitality and community well-being.

Importing the Study Area
We will use Master Plan 2019 Subzone (No Sea) for our study area. The following code chunk will import the masterplan data, removes the Z (elevation) and M (measure) diemension, and transforms into SVY21.

#|eval: false
mpsz_sf <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml") %>%

  using driver `KML'
Simple feature collection with 332 features and 2 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6057 ymin: 1.158699 xmax: 104.0885 ymax: 1.470775

The following code chunk will be use to filter the unwanted areas as we will be focused on the main island of Singapore.

#|eval: false
extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

mpsz_sf <- mpsz_sf %>%
  mutate(
    REGION_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),
    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
  ) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())

mpsz_cl <- mpsz_sf %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N != "SOUTHERN GROUP",
         PLN_AREA_N != "WESTERN ISLANDS",
         PLN_AREA_N != "NORTH-EASTERN ISLANDS")

          "data/rds/mpsz_cl.rds")

pa_sf <- mpsz_ok |>
  group_by(PLN_AREA_N, REGION_N) |>
  summarise(.groups = "drop")

st_agr(pa_sf) <- "constant"

tmap_mode("view")

tm_basemap("CartoDB.Positron") +
  tm_shape(pa_sf, name = "Planning Areas") +
    tm_polygons(
      fill       = "grey90",      # single color (OK in v4)
      fill_alpha = 0.15,          # v4: use fill_alpha (not alpha)
      border.col = "grey50",
      lwd        = 0.6,
      id         = "PLN_AREA_N",  # tooltip on hover (still supported)
      popup.vars = c("Planning Area" = "PLN_AREA_N",
                     "Region"        = "REGION_N")
    ) +

    tm_borders(col = "grey80", lwd = 0.3) +

Geocoding
For geocoding, location information can be derived directly from the postal_code. The following code chunks will be used to extract the unique postal code from the postal_code field and append the location information into the individual objects and finally convert them into a dataframe.

CafesClinicsMinimarts



biz_56112_postcode <- unique(biz_56112$postal_code)

url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search"

found <- data.frame()
not_found <- data.frame(postcode = character())

for (pc in biz_56112_postcode) {
  query <- list(
    searchVal = pc,
    returnGeom = "Y",
    getAddrDetails = "Y",
    pageNum = "1"
  )
  
  res <- GET(url, query = query)
  json <- content(res)
  
  if (json$found != 0) {
    df <- as.data.frame(json$results, stringAsFactors = FALSE)
    df$input_postcode <- pc
    found <- bind_rows(found, df)
  } else{
    not_found <- bind_rows(not_found, data.frame(postcode = pc))
  }
}


biz_56112 = biz_56112 %>%
  left_join(found,
            by = c('postal_code' = 'POSTAL'))

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Good
section: Spatial Kernel Density Estimation using Automatic Bandwidth Selection
text:
Spatial Kernel Density Estimation using Automatic Bandwidth Selection
Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is a valuable tool for visualising and analyzing first-order spatial point patterns. It is widely considered a method within Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA) because it’s used to visualize and understand spatial data patterns by transforms discrete point data.
As the default unit of measurement of SVY21 is in meters, we will have rescale the unit of measurement from meters to kilometers for all ppp files.

cafesSG_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(
  cafesSG_ppp, 1000, "km")

clinicsSG_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(
  clinicsSG_ppp, 1000, "km")

minisSG_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(
  minisSG_ppp, 1000, "km")

We estimate first-order intensity using a Gaussian kernel because kernel shape has minor influence relative to bandwidth and Gaussian yields smooth, reproducible maps and its the default for spatstat. For bandwidth, we will be using automatic bandwidth selection using both bw.diggle() and bw.ppl() for comparison.
Alternatives like bw.CvL() are valid but can be sensitive in clustered data with duplicate coordinates, while bw.scott() is a rule-of-thumb not tailored to spatial point processes.

CafesClinicsMinimarts



kde_cafes_diggle <- density(
  cafesSG_ppp_km,
  sigma = bw.diggle,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian")

kde_cafes_ppl <- density(
  cafesSG_ppp_km,
  sigma = bw.ppl,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian")

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(kde_cafes_diggle, main = "bw.diggle")
plot(kde_cafes_ppl, main = "bw.ppl")








Both selectors pick the same main hotspot in the south–central area (CBD). The bw.ppl map is smoother and more consolidated, showing a few broad blobs while bw.diggle is finer-grained, with many small, speckled highs.



kde_clinics_diggle <- density(
  clinicsSG_ppp_km,
  sigma = bw.diggle,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian")

kde_clinics_ppl <- density(
  clinicsSG_ppp_km,
  sigma = bw.ppl,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian")

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(kde_clinics_diggle, main = "bw.diggle")
plot(kde_clinics_ppl, main = "bw.ppl")








Both maps highlight a south–central to south-eastern areas as the main hotspot, with weaker scatter across the rest of the island.



kde_minis_diggle <- density(
  minisSG_ppp_km,
  sigma = bw.diggle,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian")

kde_minis_ppl <- density(
  minisSG_ppp_km,
  sigma = bw.ppl,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian")

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(kde_minis_diggle, main = "bw.diggle")
plot(kde_minis_ppl, main = "bw.ppl")








Both maps show an island-wide, heartland-driven footprint with stronger activity around major towns such as Tampines, Bishan, Jurong and Yishun.

We adopt bw.ppl() instead of bw.diggle() because it offers greater stability and interpretability for our dataset, which often contains clustered or duplicate addresses. While bw.diggle() tends to select smaller bandwidths, producing speckled surfaces with sharp micro-peaks, bw.ppl() typically yields a slightly larger and smoother bandwidth, resulting in cleaner and communication-ready density surfaces. From a planning perspective, the smoother estimates from bw.ppl() align better with analysis conducted at the planning area or subzone level, avoiding the overemphasis on very local spikes that may arise from bw.diggle().
The following code chunks will be used to plot the KDE map of each business type.

Spatio-Temporal KDE
The saptio-temporal KDE will show us the the intensity of new registrations as a function of both location and time. This should reveal the hotspots of business openings in the specific months.
We will first rescale our owin file to kilometers with the following code chunk

sg_owin_km <- rescale.owin(sg_owin, s = 1000, unitname = "km")

section: Visualizing Distribution of Businesses by Month
text:
Visualizing Distribution of Businesses by Month
The following code chunk will be used to split the distribution points into their months.

# Cafes
cafes_m <- cafes %>%
  mutate(
    DayOfYear = yday(date),
    Month_num = month(date),
    Month_fac = factor(format(floor_date(date, "month"), "%Y-%m"))
  )

# Clinics
clinics_m <- clinics %>%
  mutate(
    DayOfYear = yday(date),
    Month_num = month(date),
    Month_fac = factor(format(floor_date(date, "month"), "%Y-%m"))
  )

# Mini-marts
minis_m <- minis %>%
  mutate(
    DayOfYear = yday(date),
    Month_num = month(date),
    Month_fac = factor(format(floor_date(date, "month"), "%Y-%m"))
  )

We will next plot the distribution points per month for each business type.

CafesClinicsMinimarts



tm_shape(mpsz_cl) + tm_polygons() +
tm_shape(cafes_m) + tm_dots(size = 0.1) +
tm_facets(by = "Month_fac", free.coords = FALSE, drop.units = TRUE) +
tm_title("Cafes — monthly point distribution")











tm_shape(mpsz_cl) + tm_polygons() +
tm_shape(clinics_m) + tm_dots(size = 0.1) +
tm_facets(by = "Month_fac", free.coords = FALSE, drop.units = TRUE) +
tm_title("Clinics — monthly point distribution")











tm_shape(mpsz_cl) + tm_polygons() +
tm_shape(minis_m) + tm_dots(size = 0.1) +
tm_facets(by = "Month_fac", free.coords = FALSE, drop.units = TRUE) +
tm_title("Mini-marts — monthly point distribution")











The following code chunk will be used to extract the mark field and geometry field from the input sf data frame since these are the only information needed for as.ppp().

cafes_month <- cafes %>%
  mutate(YearMonth = floor_date(date, "month"),
         Month_num = as.integer(factor(format(YearMonth, "%Y-%m")))) %>%
  select(Month_num)

clinics_month <- clinics %>%
  mutate(YearMonth = floor_date(date, "month"),
         Month_num = as.integer(factor(format(YearMonth, "%Y-%m")))) %>%
  select(Month_num)

minis_month <- minis %>%
  mutate(YearMonth = floor_date(date, "month"),
         Month_num = as.integer(factor(format(YearMonth, "%Y-%m")))) %>%
  select(Month_num)

After we have extracted the data required, we can proceed to create the ppp files for each business type.

cafes_month_ppp <- as.ppp(cafes_month)
clinics_month_ppp <- as.ppp(clinics_month)
minis_month_ppp   <- as.ppp(minis_month)

We will then combine the ppp and owin objects.

cafes_month_owin <- cafes_month_ppp[sg_owin]
clinics_month_owin  <- clinics_month_ppp[sg_owin]
minis_month_owin  <- minis_month_ppp[sg_owin]

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Good
section: Analysing Spatial Point Process Using L-Function
text:
Analysing Spatial Point Process Using L-Function
The L-function will be used as it is often preferred in applied spatial point pattern analysis because it is a variance-stabilized transformation of Ripley’s K-function. While the K-function provides insights into clustering or dispersion across scales, it grows quadratically with distance which can make interpretation less intuitive. The L-function linearizes this growth, so under complete spatial randomness (CSR), the expectation is approximately a straight line. This makes deviations easier to interpret with positive values indicate clustering and negative values indicate dispersion.
G-function (nearest neighbor distribution) focuses only on the distance to the nearest point, making it useful for micro-scale clustering but limited in capturing patterns at broader distances.
F-function (empty space distribution) measures the distribution of distances from arbitrary locations to the nearest point, good for understanding coverage, but not as robust for detecting clustering across scales.
K-function provides the same information as L but is harder to interpret due to quadratic growth.
With that, the L-function gives the best balance of interpretability, comparability across scales, and robustness, making it the most suitable for the current analysis.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Good
section: Preparing spatio-temporal point process object of stpp
text:
Preparing spatio-temporal point process object of stpp
We will use the following code chunk to create the stpp object of each business types. The top is a simple function created so there is no need to repeat the codes.

t0 <- as.Date("2024-01-01")
as_stpp <- function(x_sf, date_col = "date") {
  coords <- st_coordinates(x_sf) / 1000
  df <- data.frame(
    x = coords[, 1],
    y = coords[, 2],
    t = as.integer(x_sf[[date_col]] - t0)
  )
  stpp::as.3dpoints(df)
}

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Good
text:
Computing spatio-temporal k-function
The following code chunk will be used to compute space-time inhomogeneous K-function for each business type.

cafes_stik <- STIKhat(cafes_stpp)
clinics_stik <- STIKhat(clinics_stpp)
minis_stik <- STIKhat(minis_stpp)

Next, plotK() is used to visualise the output space-time inhomogeneous K-function.

CafesClinicsMinimarts



plotK(cafes_stik)

The STIK plot for cafes shows higher intensity values (up to 70,000) at longer spatial and temporal lags. This suggests that cafes tend to exhibit stronger space–time clustering, meaning their openings or activities are not only concentrated in certain geographic areas but also occur close together in time. In other words, new cafes are more likely to appear near existing ones and within a relatively short time window. This could reflect competitive or lifestyle-driven clustering in high-demand zones



plotK(clinics_stik)

The STIK plot for clinics shows lower intensity compared to cafes (peaking around 50,000), but the contour lines are still tightly packed at larger distances and times. This indicates that while clinics also display spatio-temporal clustering, the effect is less pronounced than for cafes. Clinics may still co-locate in residential areas or medical hubs, but the temporal clustering is less sharp. Clinic openings may be more staggered, possibly due to regulatory or planning constraints.



plotK(minis_stik)

For minimarts, the STIK plot peaks at around 60,000, showing a clustering effect in both space and time, but not as strong or widespread as cafes. The contours suggest moderate clustering: minimarts tend to appear close to each other and often within similar timeframes, but the intensity is less extreme. This aligns with their role as convenience-focused outlets, filling gaps in residential or neighborhood demand rather than clustering as aggressively as cafes.
